strengths: Novel and practically relevant problem formulation: While distractor removal has been widely studied in scene-specific optimization (e.g., RobustNeRF, SpotlessSplats), this is the first work to systematically explore distractor-free reconstruction in feedforward generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting.

Well-motivated method tailored to feedforward settings: The reference-based mask filtering leverages the observation that re-rendered reference views are relatively stable, successfully mitigating the issue of high-loss static regions being mistakenly pruned during cross-scene training.
Comprehensive two-stage inference design: The proposed reference scoring and 3D Gaussian distractor pruning effectively handle residual artifacts and occlusions at test time.

Solid empirical performance: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets (RobustNeRF, On-the-go) and synthetic datasets demonstrate significant quantitative gains in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over baseline models and adaptations of existing distractor-removal techniques.
weaknesses: Inference assumptions on view availability: The reference scoring mechanism assumes access to a candidate pool of $K$ views ($K > N$) to select the cleanest $N$ views. In typical sparse-view generalizable 3DGS benchmarks, only $N$ views are strictly provided. While the pruning stage functions when $K=N$, the dependency on having clean candidate views in the pool should be more transparently analyzed.

Lack of direct quantitative evaluation for distractor masks: Although qualitative mask predictions are shown in Figure 6 and claimed to outperform scene-specific methods, datasets like RobustNeRF provide distractor ground-truth annotations. Reporting quantitative segmentation metrics (e.g., mIoU, precision, recall) would substantially strengthen the claim of superior mask prediction.

Reliance on heavy pre-trained modules: The pipeline heavily depends on pre-trained entity segmentation (Entity Segmentation [22]). Although masks can be pre-computed/cached during training, this increases complexity and inference runtime as acknowledged in the efficiency section.

Writing and presentation polish: There are frequent minor grammatical and formatting issues throughout the manuscript (e.g., consistently using 'distractor' instead of plural 'distractors', 'a Inference framework', and missing punctuation in citations/figure references like 'Fig.3 6' and 'Eq. 4 6 7 8').

strengths: Novel and practically relevant problem formulation: While distractor removal in scene-specific NeRF/3DGS and generalizable feed-forward 3DGS have each been studied separately, tackling transient distractors in feed-forward, generalizable 3DGS is timely and practically important for in-the-wild captures.

Well-motivated insights: The paper correctly identifies why standard loss-residual heuristic masking from per-scene optimization fails in generalizable settings (due to cross-scene inter-iteration loss variance confounding hard static regions with distractors), and smartly leverages multi-view consistency of reference-rendered static regions to guide mask prediction.

Comprehensive framework: The proposed pipeline systematically tackles both training challenges (reference-based mask filtering, disparity error decoupling, auxiliary occlusion loss) and test-time challenges (reference scoring and 3D Gaussian primitive pruning).

Solid empirical performance: Extensive experiments across real-world distractor datasets (RobustNeRF, On-the-go) and synthetic datasets demonstrate clear quantitative and qualitative advantages over adapting existing scene-specific distractor removal methods into generalizable 3DGS.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on external 2D entity segmentation priors: The mask refinement and pruning heavily depend on an off-the-shelf Entity Segmentation model (Qi et al., 2022). It remains unclear how robust the system is when the 2D segmenter encounters out-of-domain distractor types or failure cases.

Inference computational overhead: The two-stage inference framework requires coarse reconstruction, scoring candidate views, and pruning. While Table 5 reports rendering time (0.148s/0.111s), it assumes pre-computed segmentation masks; the actual end-to-end inference latency including 2D segmentation on un-cached test frames should be explicitly discussed.

Potential sensitivity to geometry/depth estimation errors: The reference-to-query warping Wi->T relies on rasterized depth Di from predicted Gaussians. Early during training or in complex geometry with wide baselines, depth errors could propagate into erroneous mask filtering and disparity decoupling.

Minor presentation and editorial issues: There are several formatting irregularities and minor typos throughout the paper (e.g., 'Eq. 4 6 7 8' on page 5, 'Segmantation' in Table 2, and slightly cramped figure layouts in Figures 4 and 9).

strengths: Novel and practically relevant problem formulation: While distractor removal has been extensively studied in per-scene NeRF/3DGS optimization, handling transient distractors in feedforward, generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting across unseen scenes is an important and unexplored direction.

Technically sound training design: The proposed reference-based mask prediction intuitively exploits the observation that non-distractor regions re-rendered from reference views maintain geometric consistency, effectively preventing the over-masking of hard-to-reconstruct static regions typical of heuristic loss-thresholding methods.

Well-motivated inference strategy: Decoupling disparity errors from transient distractors, paired with two-stage candidate reference scoring and explicit 3D Gaussian pruning, provides an effective pipeline to clean up novel view syntheses without requiring extensive per-scene fine-tuning.

Comprehensive empirical validation and ablations: The manuscript benchmarks against several adapted state-of-the-art distractor handling methods (e.g., RobustNeRF, NeRF-HuGS, SLS) on real and synthetic datasets, providing clear component-by-component ablations for both the training and inference modules.
weaknesses: Scale and diversity of the training data: The model is primarily trained on a small set of outdoor scenes from the On-the-go dataset. Standard generalizable 3DGS models typically rely on large-scale datasets (e.g., RealEstate10K) to learn robust cross-scene geometry; demonstrating generalizability when trained on such a limited number of scenes raises questions about scalability and coverage across diverse scene distributions.

Reliance on pre-trained 2D segmentation: The pipeline depends heavily on pre-trained Entity Segmentation (HQ-SAM) to define object boundaries and fill warped masks. The failure modes and sensitivity of the framework when the 2D segmenter encounters out-of-distribution entities or cluttered boundaries are not thoroughly discussed.

Altered inference setting: The reference scoring mechanism assumes access to a pre-captured candidate pool of K images from which N images are selected. While practical in some capture setups, this shifts the task slightly from standard sparse-view feedforward reconstruction (fixed input views) to view-selection plus reconstruction.

Clarity, grammar, and presentation: The paper suffers from frequent grammatical errors, awkward sentence structures, and minor typographical mistakes (e.g., 'Segmantation' in Table 2, inconsistent pluralization of 'distractor/distractors', and incomplete figure references such as 'Fig.3 6'). The manuscript requires careful proofreading and language polishing.

strengths: Pioneering and timely formulation: The paper addresses distractor-free reconstruction within the generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) paradigm, bridging the gap between scene-specific distractor removal methods and feed-forward novel view synthesis.

Insightful method design: Leveraging the stability of re-rendered reference views to guide query distractor mask filtering (based on static 3D consistency) is well-motivated and empirically validated by the training dynamics analysis in Table 6.

Decoupling disparity errors from transient objects: Explicitly isolating camera disparity-induced errors at image margins from actual transient distractors prevents erroneous suppression of valid static scene content.

Thorough empirical validation: The framework is evaluated across real datasets (On-the-go, RobustNeRF) and synthetic datasets, demonstrating consistent improvements over generalizable baselines (PixelSplat, MVSplat) and baselines retrofitted with scene-specific distractor-handling losses.
weaknesses: Evaluation conducted at very low resolution: Experiments are primarily performed at a downsampled resolution of 192x256. Transient distractors and fine-grained geometry often behave differently at full resolutions typically benchmarked in RobustNeRF and On-the-go, making it unclear whether the mask filtering and rasterization hold up equally well on high-resolution data.

Inference view selection assumption: The two-stage inference framework assumes access to a pool of K candidate views (K > N) to score and filter down to cleaner references. While practical in dense video captures, in standard feed-forward benchmark settings where only fixed N sparse views are provided, the inference gains rely purely on pruning without reference re-selection.

Mathematical clarity in Distractor Pruning: The mechanism for pruning 3D Gaussian primitives in Section 4.2 is described purely textually. A precise mathematical formulation detailing how 3D Gaussians are indexed, mapped back to multi-view 2D reference masks, and pruned—especially under partial occlusions and anisotropic primitive extents—would improve reproducibility and rigor.

Writing and typographical polish: The paper suffers from frequent grammatical inaccuracies (e.g., repeatedly using 'distractor' instead of plural 'distractors', 'candidator', 'segmantation' in Table 2, 'Cclustering' in Section B.4, and 'REPRODICIBILITY' in the section header).

strengths: Novel and highly practical problem formulation: Addressing transient distractors in feed-forward, generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) bridges an important gap between generalizable novel view synthesis and in-the-wild captures.

Well-motivated technical insight: The core observation that re-rendered reference static regions are inherently more stable than query views is effectively leveraged to prevent the over-masking problem common in residual-based robust optimization.

Comprehensive framework: The proposed pipeline methodically handles both training (reference-based mask filtering, disparity decoupling, auxiliary occlusion loss) and inference (reference scoring/selection and 3D Gaussian distractor pruning).

Solid empirical results: The method shows consistent quantitative and qualitative gains across real-world datasets (RobustNeRF, On-the-go) and synthetic datasets, clearly outperforming both naive generalizable baselines and baselines adapted with existing scene-specific distractor removal methods.
Thorough ablation studies: The paper extensively ablates individual components (mask filtering, refinement, auxiliary loss, reference scoring, pruning, and choice of segmentation model).
weaknesses: Inference reference pool assumption: The full DGGS inference pipeline assumes access to a larger pool of candidate views ($K \ge N$) to score and re-select the cleanest $N$ views. While realistic for video captures, this deviates from the standard sparse-view evaluation protocol where only a fixed set of $N$ views is provided. While DGGS-TR works without this pool, a non-trivial portion of the final performance boost relies on this selection mechanism.

Sensitivity to depth estimation accuracy: The reference-to-query warping of masks relies heavily on the depth maps ($D_i$) predicted by the coarse/intermediate generalizable 3DGS. In early training iterations or scenes with complex, thin, or low-texture geometry, depth errors could propagate into imprecise warped masks.

Clarity and presentation issues: The manuscript contains multiple grammatical errors, typos, and awkward phrasings (e.g., consistent use of singular 'distractor' where plural 'distractors' is meant, 'candidator' instead of 'candidate', 'REPRODICIBILITY' header typo, and mixed set/binary notation such as $\{\cap_{i=1}^N M_{Qry_i}\} \cup M_{Rob}$).

Computational overhead: While inference remains faster than scene-specific per-scene optimization, incorporating multi-view warping, pre-trained segmentation models, and two-stage inference increases latency compared to standard feed-forward generalizable 3DGS models.

strengths: Formulates an important and timely problem: extending distractor-free reconstruction to feed-forward, generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, moving beyond computationally heavy per-scene optimization.
The core insight of exploiting reference view re-rendering consistency to differentiate true transient distractors from difficult-to-reconstruct static regions is intuitive and well-motivated.

The proposed inference framework—combining mask-based reference scoring for cleaner view selection and 3D Gaussian primitive pruning—provides noticeable qualitative and quantitative improvements over naively applying generalizable 3DGS.

Provides extensive experimental analysis, including retraining existing robust/distractor-free loss formulations on generalizable baselines, ablations on training components, and synthetic test scenarios.
weaknesses: Questionable training scale for 'generalizable' models: The training set for the retrained models consists only of 10 outdoor sequences from the On-the-go dataset. Standard generalizable 3DGS models (e.g., MVSplat, pixelSplat) rely on thousands of diverse scenes (e.g., RE10K) to learn generalizable multi-view geometry. Training on only 10 scenes explains the massive drop in baseline performance (MVSplat falling from 20.03 dB to 15.45 dB) and raises doubts about true out-of-distribution generalizability.

Very low image resolution: All experiments are downsampled to 192 x 256, which is substantially below standard benchmarks in 3DGS (typically 512 x 512 or higher). It remains unclear whether the depth-warping and heuristic rasterization thresholds scale robustly to higher resolutions.

Reliance on a dense candidate pool during inference: The two-stage inference framework assumes access to a pool of K candidate reference images (e.g., K=8) to select the top N=4 cleanest views. In standard sparse-view feed-forward settings where only N views are provided, the reference scoring component cannot function, limiting the practical applicability of the inference pipeline.

Significant dependence on heavy external 2D segmentation models (Entity Segmentation / SAM / SAM2) and hand-tuned heuristic thresholds (e.g., kernel operators, warping thresholds, residual loss cutoff rho).

Writing and presentation issues: Persistent grammatical errors throughout the paper (notably using 'distractor' exclusively as a singular/uncountable noun across sentences, typos like 'candidator', 'Cclustering', 'REPRODICIBILITY'), along with mismatched figure citations (e.g., referencing Figure 16 on page 19 when discussing mask comparisons, whereas Figure 16 actually depicts failure cases).
